title: Search Tree Value Nearest a Target
statement:
You get the root of a non-empty binary search tree with distinct integer values, and a number target that may have a fractional part.

Return the value in the tree that is closest to target. If two values are equally close, return the smaller one.

examples.why: 6 is 0.6 away; the next closest, 8, is 1.4 away.
10 and 12 are both 1 away. On a tie the smaller value wins.
Far past the largest value, so the answer is the rightmost node.

hints: You could visit every node and keep the closest. What does the search-tree order let you skip?
At a node, if target is smaller than its value, every value in the right subtree is even farther away. Which way should you go?
Walk down from the root like a binary search, going left or right toward target, and update the best answer at every node you pass. The closest value is always on that path.

explain.intuition:
In a search tree, a single walk from the root toward target passes every value that could be closest. At a node with value v > target, everything to the right is even bigger, so even farther from the target. Only the left side could hold something closer. The mirror case goes right.

So walk down like a binary search and keep the best value seen. The closest value is either the largest value below target or the smallest value above it, and both of those are on the search path. That gives O(h) time instead of O(n).
steps: While node is not null: compare |node.val − target| with |best − target|. If it is smaller, or equal and node.val < best, set best = node.val.
Move to node.left if target < node.val, otherwise to node.right.
pitfalls: Ignoring the tie rule. With target 11 and both 10 and 12 present, the answer must be 10.
Stopping at the first node whose value is within 1 of the target. A closer value can still be deeper down.
Rounding the target to an integer first. With target 4.5, the values 3 and 6 are 1.5 away each and 3 wins the tie, but after rounding to 5 the 6 looks closer.

complexity.time: O(h), where h is the tree height

solutions.title: Visit every node
solutions.idea: Walk the whole tree and keep the closest value, breaking ties toward the smaller one.

solutions.title: Walk one path down the tree
solutions.idea: Move toward the target like a binary search; the closest value is always on that path.

followups: Return the k values closest to the target, in any order. Can you beat O(n) when k is small?
Many targets arrive one after another for the same tree. What would you precompute?
